status_summary: The Office of China Coordination remains in place within State's Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs. State's Foreign Affairs Manual chapter on the bureau (last revised 2025-03-25) lists the office, headed by a China Coordinator who is also a deputy assistant secretary, reporting through the bureau to the Under Secretary for Political Affairs and also to the Deputy Secretary; that section's text dates from 2023, and the chapter still lists an office that was closed in July 2025, so it may not reflect later changes. World Journal reported on 2025-07-25, citing officials, that Joshua Young, then a deputy assistant secretary for international security policy, would take over the office as its fourth coordinator since 2022 and would report directly to the Under Secretary for Political Affairs rather than through the bureau's assistant secretary; Taiwan News reported the same appointment on 2025-07-31, citing Nikkei Asia, with an unnamed State official describing it as elevating the department's focus on China, but did not state the reporting line. A House bill introduced on 2025-09-11 (H.R. 5329) describes the office as an existing part of the East Asia bureau. At the same time, the July 2025 reduction in force closed a different East Asia office, the Office of Multilateral Affairs, which covered ASEAN and South China Sea issues, with State saying its functions would be integrated elsewhere. No State announcement of the 2025 appointment or document on the office's current staffing was found.

timeline.event: State's Foreign Affairs Manual chapter on the East Asia bureau (1 FAM 130, last revised this date) lists the Office of China Coordination (China House), headed by a China Coordinator who is also a deputy assistant secretary and reports to the bureau's Assistant Secretary, through the bureau to the Under Secretary for Political Affairs, and to the Deputy Secretary; the China section text is dated 2023-10-23.
timeline.source: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Affairs Manual

timeline.event: NPR reported that the July 2025 reduction in force closed State's Office of Multilateral Affairs in the East Asia bureau, which covered ASEAN and South China Sea issues; State said mission-critical functions would be integrated elsewhere.

World Journal reported, citing officials, that Joshua Young would lead the Office of China Coordination and report directly to the Under Secretary for Political Affairs, with the office remaining in the East Asia bureau.

Taiwan News, citing Nikkei Asia, reported that Joshua Young was appointed head of the Office of China Coordination and deputy assistant secretary for China and Taiwan, quoting an unnamed State official that the department was looking to elevate its focus on China; it does not state a reporting line.

H.R. 5329, the Regional China Officer Authorization Act, was introduced and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee; it would establish a unit inside the Office of China Coordination in the East Asia bureau.

title: Support and keep a centralized China policy office at State (China House)
uncertainties: The 2025 appointment rests on two news reports: World Journal (Chinese-language, citing unnamed officials) and Taiwan News (citing Nikkei Asia and an unnamed State official); only World Journal states the direct reporting line to the Under Secretary. State's Foreign Affairs Manual lists the office, but its China section is dated 2023-10-23 and the chapter still lists the Office of Multilateral Affairs that NPR reported closed in July 2025, so the manual lags the reorganization. A Paraguayan government news agency headline dated 2026-05-05 refers to a meeting with State's coordinator for China affairs, but the page could not be opened, so continuation into 2026 is not confirmed. A National Review commentary of 2025-04-29 said the April 2025 reorganization offered no China-specific reforms. Inference: the Mandate asks only that the concept be supported with adjustments, so keeping the office and naming a new head is rated implemented at the band floor, with match partial because the staffing and interagency concerns the text raises are not shown to be addressed.
